accuracy.evidence: Every form checked against the CCSS L.5.1 language standards and standard grammar references (Cambridge Grammar of English; Biber et al.): past progressive for an action in progress at a past moment (was cooking at 6), past perfect for completion before a past moment and the earlier of two past events (had started, had gone, had fed), present perfect for a period up to now (has lived, have known), simple past for a finished period (lived 2015–2018), future progressive and future perfect (will be watching, will have finished). Conditionals: first (if + present, will), zero (if + present, present), second with were-subjunctive (if I were, would), third (if + had + past participle, would have) with its counterfactual meaning. The flashback paragraph was rewritten so no past perfect is used without a past reference point. Numeric items enumerated at range corners by validate_lessons.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented errors for this standard: reading event order from word order rather than tense (FIRST sentences 3 and 4 tell the earlier event last; challenge tags arrived/both; p1), confusing progressive and perfect (scene wrong-choice messages, tags hadread/read, m1), simple past vs present perfect (scene 3 and 4, step 1 predict 'No, that time is over', tags over/future, m2), reading would have as factual (step 2 predict 'Yes', tags won/later, p5), and over-correcting legitimate shifts in dialogue (step 3 predict 'Yes, change it to loved', the love token, m6) as well as inconsistent shifts (tags smiles/leave, m5).

lab_distinct.evidence: gate_lab_distinct passed (under 30% similar to every flagship lab). Earlier tense labs place sentences on a yesterday/now line (411 flagtense), build has/have + participle (756) or helpers for -ing (806). This lab is about choosing between forms for meaning: deciding which of two past events came first from had alone, matching a verb form to a described state (in progress, finished, up to now, over) across past, present and future, sorting conditionals by reality, and repairing slips while defending a correct shift in speech.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner discovers the rule from contrast: the same cinema sentence with and without had gives opposite orders; each scene offers two near-miss forms whose feedback names what they would mean (had cooked = already finished, but the soup is bubbling); the conditional sort shows will/would/would have mapping to real/imagined/did not happen; tapping 'love' to fix it is refused with the reason; the timeline step makes them read four tenses to order Kai's paragraph.

predictions.evidence: Four locked predictions, each with a tempting wrong option that the lab disproves: 'We got to the cinema' first (word order), 'No, that time is over' for has lived, 'Yes' I caught the bus for a third conditional, and 'Yes, change it to loved' for present-tense speech. A.reveal reports each prediction in the done message.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six challenge questions with every wrong answer tagged: arrived/both (had left marks the earlier event), hadread/read (in progress needs was + -ing), over/future (present perfect runs up to now), won/later (would have = did not happen), real/pastcond (which conditional is imagined now), smiles/leave (fix to opened rather than shifting the other verb). In the lab every wrong verb tile has its own message naming what that form would mean.

readability.evidence: Kid text Flesch-Kincaid 2.8 (limit 6.5), adult 7.4 (limit 9.5). The curriculum terms progressive, perfect, past participle, past perfect, present perfect and conditional are each introduced with a worked example sentence. Canvas text is one sentence per card; buttons name their action (First: The film started, Fix "runs", the box names).

no_filler.evidence: gate_content found no filler phrases and explanation similarity under 12% to every lesson (including 411, 756 and 806). Each kid paragraph adds one idea: what tense can say, progressive vs perfect vs simple, the past perfect and conditionals, and consistency with the speech exception. Adult text gives standards fit, the task list and named mistakes with one question to ask.

mobile.evidence: Checked iPhone 13 and desktop screenshots of every step before and after Show me (.tmp_run/shots/ts-*). On a phone the three verb tiles stack full width at 52 px tall with 16 px text; event chips are about 160 × 64 px; the story words wrap inside the canvas with verbs as 36 px tall pills; the conditional boxes are three 100 px columns with wrapped labels; the timeline step uses two columns of four 50 px rows; feedback wraps inside the canvas.

accessibility.evidence: walk.cjs passed on desktop and iPhone 13: all five tasks complete with Show me, challenge shown, axe WCAG 2.1 AA clean in both themes, no console errors. Every drag or tap has a button (First: event, each verb, the three box names, Fix "verb", each event). The canvas aria-label reads the sentence and events, the scene and choices, the current conditional, the story with the verbs to check, or the timeline so far after every action; messages are spoken with c.say.
